sentences.text: Provo Canyon School is a locked residential treatment center for teenagers in Utah County, Utah, founded in 1971 and owned since 2000 by Universal Health Services (UHS), one of the country's largest for-profit behavioral health companies.

sentences.text: The first legal challenge came from two boys the school held for other states' juvenile courts.
On September 21, 1978, Timothy Milonas Jr., sent by a Nevada court, and Kenneth Rice, sent by an Alaska court, filed a federal class action against the owners, Williams, Crist and later Thorne.
The court found that the school read and censored boys' mail, gave them polygraph tests, locked them in isolation rooms and used excessive force, including the "hair dance," a grip on a boy's hair.

In 1980 a jury found for the owners on damages, but the judge permanently barred polygraphs and mail opening, and allowed isolation and physical restraint only to contain a violent boy or in immediate danger.

sources.cite: The Salt Lake Tribune, Sep 20, 2020 (via Center for Health Journalism)

sentences.text: On September 13, 1982, the Tenth Circuit upheld the injunction.
It ruled that the state was so involved in the school that it was "a joint participant," and that the practices violated the boys' due process and First Amendment rights.
Complaints continued under Charter.
In September 1990 the school suspended a staff member accused of having sex with a 15-year-old girl four times, and Provo police looked into claims involving other students.
David Taylor, admitted from October 1990 to August 1991, sued in 1995 for fraud, medical negligence and false imprisonment.

sources.cite: Taylor v. Charter Medical Corp., 162 F.3d 827 (5th Cir. 1998)

sentences.text: A jury found the school 25 percent at fault and it was held liable for $7,500.

Utah put the Provo campus on conditional status.

sentences.text: On October 9, 2020, she led several hundred survivors to the school's front gates.
The school said it could not comment on anything before its owners bought it in 2000.
On February 8, 2021, Hilton testified for Senate Bill 127, which allowed surprise inspections of youth treatment centers and required them to report restraints.
The bill passed the legislature that March.
In August 2021 Aaron Ross, who was sent there at 13 in 2001, sued the school, UHS and three staff members in federal court in New York.

The case was moved to federal court in Utah in January 2022.

sentences.text: The violence continued.
On March 27, 2023, a resident at the Springville campus punched a staff member, who later died after surgery; police had been called to the campus eight times between February and April.
In September 2024 staff member Mulimauga Tuiloma punched a 15-year-old girl in the face and told police he had been using a restraint technique.
He pleaded guilty to child abuse, and in July 2025 he was given a suspended jail sentence and probation.
State licensers found that staff harmed residents in September 2024, restrained one unnecessarily that November, and struck a teenager being restrained in December.

It was the seventh time in two years that they had found the Springville program failed to keep young people safe, and in February 2025 they put conditions on its license, which covered 120 residents.
On April 13, 2025, licensers later found, a staff member at the Springville campus who did not follow the school's Handle With Care restraint policy injured a client's face during a restraint.

sentences.text: On July 17 it revoked the Provo campus license and ordered all services there stopped by August 16, citing failures to protect clients from harm and the use of cruel and unnecessary practices.

Hilton said the state had "confirmed what survivors have known all along," and in August she urged Utah not to let the school reopen.

testimony.text: As a licensed professional, Registered Nurse, under duty of obligation under the laws of California I am writing this to document and report suspected and actual child abuse both physical, emotional, psychological, sexual as well as the suspected and actual abuse of children in the custody and care of (staff) at Provo Canyon School. … SUMMARY OF ABUSE SUFFERED BY OUR CHILD: Assault, battery, hair pulled, restrained against her will, drugged with an overdose of Haldol which caused her to black out and wake to blindness, facial paralysis and pain, drooling and lethargy for three days. Imprisoned and forced to sit in structure (staring straight ahead) for up to 5 hours. … We were told by cell-phone message on or about January 10, that the case was going to be closed because the attorneys from the Utah Valley DA believed that these abuses were not criminal but contractual and civil in nature.
testimony.who: Parent, from a complaint to Utah authorities

testimony.text: I have been thrown on a concrete floor with a knee in my back crushing my lungs and someone's knee of my neck, someone sitting on my arms and then another sitting with their knees on my legs, just to make sure I wouldn't move when given a shot of Haldol, all because I just yelled out loud in my frustrations in the ob's room trying to get my anger out. I've been told by a staff that they know I'm claustrophobic and then was shoved by him into the ob's room and had the door shut on me.
How can anyone justify shooting a child up with Thorazine, or sexually abusing a child, or denying a child medical attention. I've seen all these happen in my 11-month stay there in 1990-1991.
